title: Erdoğan Tells Zelenskiy Black Sea Attacks 'Inexplicable' as Ankara Pursues F-35 Green Light
subhead: President Erdoğan used a phone call with Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelenskiy to press for restraint in the Black Sea, while separately expressing fresh confidence that the US will clear Türkiye for F-35 jets. Both signals come as Ankara works a busy UN General Assembly sideline.

sections.heading: Black Sea: Erdoğan Calls Maritime Attacks 'Inexplicable'
sections.body: President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan told Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelenskiy in a phone call that attacks in the Black Sea are 'inexplicable,' Reuters reported on Thursday. The remark lands as shipping lanes have become a renewed flashpoint, with Ukraine publicly signaling readiness for a maritime truce even as grain-export tensions persist. Ankara's intervention is significant because Türkiye controls the Bosporus shipping route that is central to any Black Sea commerce arrangement and has sought to mediate between Kyiv and Moscow throughout the war.
sections.whyItMatters: Türkiye is positioning itself as the arbiter of Black Sea shipping safety, a role with direct bearing on Ukrainian grain exports and regional energy transit. Erdoğan's wording signals Ankara pushing both sides toward de-escalation rather than choosing a side.

sections.heading: Defense: Erdoğan Confident on F-35 Re-Entry
sections.body: Erdoğan said Thursday he is 'confident' Türkiye will get US F-35 fighter jets, according to Daily Sabah. The statement extends a months-long push to reverse Ankara's ejection from the F-35 program over its acquisition of Russian S-400 systems, and follows a July meeting in which Washington signaled willingness to lift Türkiye sanctions and discuss F-35 sales, Reuters reported. The F-35 file remains legally contested in Washington, where critics point to Türkiye's Russia and China cooperation as grounds for continued exclusion.
sections.whyItMatters: A green light on the F-35 would mark a full repair of Türkiye-US defense ties after years of rupture, but Congress and policy hawks retain blocking power. Erdoğan's public confidence signals the issue is live at the highest level of the bilateral talks.

sections.heading: Iraq: Bashiqa Base Handover and Sinjar Deal
sections.body: Türkiye and Iraq agreed to a gradual transfer of Ankara's military base at Bashiqa, northeast of Mosul, to Baghdad, the Iraqi prime minister's office announced following a Wednesday meeting between Erdoğan and Iraqi PM Ali al-Zaidi on the UNGA sidelines in New York. The statement said the two sides agreed 'on fully establishing state authority in Sinjar and ending the presence of outlawed foreign armed elements' — an apparent reference to the PKK — and pledged to expand bilateral trade and accelerate joint projects, notably the Development Road corridor. Baghdad has long viewed the base, home to up to 600 Turkish soldiers since 2015, as a breach of Iraqi sovereignty, according to Al Jazeera.
sections.whyItMatters: The handover addresses a chronic sovereignty flashpoint while preserving a Turkish security foothold narrative via the Sinjar arrangement and the Development Road project that Baghdad and Ankara both champion as a regional trade artery.

sections.heading: Foreign Relations: EU Scrutiny of Türkiye-Saudi-Pakistan Pact
sections.body: A European Union lawmaker has demanded answers on the Türkiye-Saudi Arabia-Pakistan joint defence agreement, The Brussels Times reported Thursday. The pact, signed at the recent

has drawn attention in Brussels over its implications for EU defense and Türkiye's alignment within NATO. The EU query comes amid a broader renegotiation of Türkiye-EU relations, where Ankara has pressed that 'Europe cannot be safe without Turkey,' a message Erdoğan delivered at the UN General Assembly, per Euronews.
sections.whyItMatters: The EU's questioning suggests the trilateral defense pact with two Muslim-majority states is testing Brussels' comfort with Türkiye's independent defense posture, adding a wrinkle to already-fraught Türkiye-EU ties.

sections.heading: Economy: Rate Hold, Capacity Uptick, Market Support
sections.body: Türkiye's central bank kept policy rates unchanged while flagging continued inflation risks, the Wall Street Journal reported earlier this month, and the Reuters news agency reported that Ankara stepped in to support markets in mid-September after a fund liquidity crunch sparked a selloff. In a brighter signal, Türkiye's manufacturing capacity utilization rose to 74.2% in September, per Yeni Şafak. The mixed picture underscores a stabilization effort that remains dependent on external financing and investor confidence.
sections.whyItMatters: The central bank's caution reflects an inflation fight that has yet to be won, while the September market intervention shows authorities remain prepared to defend the lira against volatility. Capacity gains offer a rare bright spot in a pressured economy.

sections.heading: Energy: Minister Warns of 'Biggest Energy Crisis in Modern History'
sections.body: Türkiye's energy minister warned the country is living through 'modern history's biggest energy crisis,' Türkiye Today reported, as regional instability — including the Iran war-driven energy crunch highlighted by Iran International this week — keeps supply chains under strain ahead of winter. Ankara has leaned on expanded domestic gas production and alternative supply routes to cushion exposure to disrupted corridors.
sections.whyItMatters: Energy cost pressures feed directly into Türkiye's inflation problem and its trade balance. How Ankara manages winter gas supplies, amid turmoil on its eastern flank, will shape both the economy and public tolerance for price rises.

bottomLine: The through-line of Thursday's Türkiye moves is a government working every track at once: mediating Black Sea shipping safety with Ukraine, pushing Washington for an F-35 restoration, cementing the Bashiqa handover and Sinjar arrangement with Iraq, and deflecting EU unease over its trilateral defense pact with Riyadh and Islamabad. The headline development is the shift on the Black Sea, where Türkiye is asserting a mediator's role even while Ukraine signals openness to a maritime truce. Ankara is simultaneously repairing its Western defense relationship and building independent partnerships, a balancing act that will be tested by winter energy pressures and the unresolved F-35 question.
sources: Reuters, Daily Sabah, Al Jazeera, Associated Press, The Jerusalem Post, Euronews, The Brussels Times, Wall Street Journal, Yeni Şafak English, Türkiye Today, Iran International, Middle East Eye
